blocks.heading: Different arrangements reward different things
blocks.text: Payment systems include salary, wages based on time or output, combination systems, bonuses, fringe benefits, commissions, productivity agreements and profit sharing. A salary commonly fixes an annual amount paid in regular instalments. Time work pays for time worked; piece work pays for acceptable units; a combination mixes a basic payment with an incentive. Bonuses are additional rewards against stated conditions. Commission links earnings to sales, while profit sharing distributes an agreed portion of profit. A productivity agreement links a negotiated improvement in output per input with rewards. Fringe benefits supply non-cash benefits. Some arrangements overlap: a salesperson can have a salary plus commission and an employer-provided service. State the base and the incentive separately, including the outcome each rewards.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Tuli Sales pays a basic amount plus a percentage of sales value. Oka Assembly pays for hours worked with a bonus for meeting an agreed quality-and-output target. The first is salary or basic pay plus commission; the second combines time work with a conditional bonus. Neither should be described as pure piece work, since neither pays solely per acceptable unit.

blocks.heading: Salaries
blocks.text: A salary is commonly stated as an annual amount paid in regular, often monthly, instalments. It is not directly calculated per item produced. Predictability can support income security and suit work where output is difficult to count. The employer gains a stable basic pay commitment, but a fixed amount gives no automatic direct reward for extra individual units. Performance can still be managed through objectives, feedback and separate incentives.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Nela Office pays an annual salary of N$120,000 in twelve equal monthly instalments. Basic monthly salary is N$10,000 before any separately stated deductions or additions. A busy month does not by itself change that contractual base.

blocks.heading: Wages
blocks.text: Wages are employee earnings commonly calculated by hours worked or units produced and paid at an agreed interval. The amount and basis depend on the system; being paid weekly does not itself prove piece work or time work. Wages can provide a transparent link to time or output, but the design must fit quality, safety and employees’ control over the measured activity. Do not confuse the pay interval with the calculation basis.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Ota Works pays workers weekly using an agreed hourly rate. The weekly interval describes when payment occurs, while hours determine the wage calculation. A different weekly worker could instead be paid per acceptable item.

blocks.heading: Piece work
blocks.text: Piece work pays an agreed amount for each acceptable unit produced. Earnings increase with qualifying output, giving a direct incentive where individual units can be counted and effort influences them. It can encourage speed, but quality, safety and cooperation may suffer if the scheme rewards quantity alone. Workers may face uncertain earnings if material shortages beyond their control stop output. Clearly define acceptable output and treatment of interruptions.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Rena Packs pays N$4 for each acceptable pack. A worker completes 80 acceptable packs. Earnings from piece work are N$320 under the stated scheme. If rejected packs earn no payment, rushing can reduce both the worker’s earnings and business quality.

blocks.heading: Time work
blocks.text: Time work pays a rate for time worked rather than directly for each item. It suits tasks whose output is difficult to attribute individually or where careful service and quality matter. It provides predictable pay for stated hours but no automatic direct output incentive, so supervision and meaningful objectives still matter. Total wages can rise with more hours; time work is not pay determined by the number of items.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Hila Repairs pays N$35 per hour for 40 normal hours, with no additional payment in this example. Wages are N$1,400. The calculation uses hours, not repairs completed. This can support careful diagnosis but does not itself show whether time was used productively.

blocks.heading: Combination systems
blocks.text: A combination system provides a basic time-based or fixed payment plus a performance-related element. The base supports income stability, while the incentive can reward specified output, sales or quality. It can balance security and effort but is more complex to administer and must specify exactly what qualifies. A poor target can encourage gaming or conflict even when a base is provided.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Teya Bags pays N$900 basic weekly pay plus N$3 for each acceptable bag above a target of 100. A worker makes 120 acceptable bags. The incentive is N$60 and total pay N$960. The base is not multiplied by output; only the twenty units above the stated threshold earn the extra payment.

blocks.heading: Bonuses
blocks.text: A bonus is an additional payment linked to stated conditions, such as meeting a target, achieving quality or contributing to a team result. It differs from ordinary basic pay. A clear attainable target can focus effort, but unclear rules or targets outside staff control can seem unfair. A team bonus can support cooperation while also creating disputes about unequal contributions. State the condition rather than assuming every bonus is paid for output alone.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Kena Assembly offers a team bonus only if its order meets both the agreed dispatch date and quality check. The conditions encourage coordination and acceptable work rather than quantity alone. Staff need to understand how the result is assessed before the work begins.

blocks.heading: Fringe benefits
blocks.text: Fringe benefits are non-monetary rewards given to employees. Examples include employer-provided meals, transport or access to a specified service. They can help recruitment, retention or practical attendance where staff value them. They cost resources and may be less attractive to employees who need spendable income or cannot use the service. A cash housing allowance is a money payment; providing accommodation is a benefit in kind. Do not classify solely from a benefit label.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Omi Farm provides a daily transport service to the workplace rather than paying a cash allowance. The service is a fringe benefit that may make attendance easier. Staff living outside its route may value it less, so the employer should assess actual access.

blocks.heading: Commissions
blocks.text: Commission is earnings linked to sales, often a percentage of qualifying sales value. It can be paid alone or with a basic salary. A direct sales reward can encourage customer contact and selling effort, but may encourage pressure selling or neglect of after-sales service if only sales value counts. Earnings can fluctuate with demand beyond the salesperson’s control. State whether commission is based on orders, paid sales or another agreed measure.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Tuli Sales pays 5% commission on qualifying sales value of N$20,000, in addition to any separately stated basic pay. Commission is N$1,000. The calculation is based on sales value, not the number of units or the salesperson’s hours. Customer service conditions can help prevent unsuitable selling.

blocks.heading: Productivity agreements
blocks.text: A productivity agreement is a negotiated arrangement linking improved output per input to an agreed reward or benefit. Workers and management agree changes in work methods and how gains will be shared. More total output is not necessarily greater productivity if labour input rises equally or faster. Clear measures, quality safeguards and a credible method of sharing gains matter. Workers may resist if they expect only more effort or fewer jobs without a fair benefit.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Naro Foods agrees a better layout and a shared reward if acceptable output per labour hour improves without extra defects. The agreement links reward to efficiency, not merely a larger total order. Jointly checking labour hours and acceptable output helps determine whether the stated condition is met.

blocks.heading: Profit sharing
blocks.text: Profit sharing distributes an agreed portion of business profit to employees under specified rules. It can encourage staff to consider overall costs, quality and cooperation rather than only individual output. However, profit depends on many factors outside one worker’s control and payments can be delayed or uncertain. The arrangement is not the same as a guaranteed wage increase or a commission on sales revenue. Workers need transparent eligibility and calculation rules.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Ruma Goods allocates 10% of annual profit N$80,000 to its employee profit-sharing pool. The pool is N$8,000, distributed under the agreed rules. It is not 10% of sales and is not N$8,000 for every worker unless that is separately stated.

blocks.heading: Worked practice: Rewards and their motivational effects
blocks.text:
Hema Stitch makes identical items with reliably available materials. Acceptable individual output can be counted and workers can influence it. It compares pure piece work with basic time pay plus a quality-and-output bonus. Staff value stable earnings. For part (b) only, the business switches to unique, complex repairs whose quality and completion time vary greatly, making comparable individual unit counts unreliable. Other facts remain unchanged.

a Evaluate the reward options at Hema under the original facts. [12]
b Evaluate the options after the change to unique repairs. Explain whether the judgement changes. [12]

a Pure piece work fits measurable identical units but exposes income to the item count and may reward rushing unless acceptance standards are clear. The combination gives a reliable base and directs a bonus at acceptable output. Choose the combination for income stability and quality, with attainable targets and fair assessment. b Unique repairs remove comparable unit counts: a worker handling a difficult repair could appear less productive than one receiving easy work. Pure piece work becomes less suitable, and the original quantity-based bonus also needs redesign. Retain basic time pay and use carefully assessed quality, customer-service or team outcomes if a bonus is feasible. The preference for a stable base holds, but the bonus measure must change because counting finished items no longer represents comparable performance.

blocks.heading: Worked practice: Rewards and their motivational effects
blocks.text:
Tano Packs makes identical packs. Individual acceptable output can be counted, workers control their pace and materials are reliably available. Management compares pure piece work with basic time pay plus an acceptable-output bonus. Staff value reliable income and the customer requires consistent quality.

a(i) State two financial rewards. [2]
a(ii) State two features of piece work. [2]
b State two non-financial rewards. [2]
c Explain why the link between acceptable output and reward matters at Tano. [6]
d Evaluate pure piece work against the proposed combination system. [8]

a(i) A cash bonus and commission. a(ii) Workers are paid an agreed rate for each acceptable unit; earnings can be uncertain because they fall if output falls. b Recognition and meaningful responsibility. c Countable individual output and control of pace let workers see how effort affects earnings. Restricting rewards to acceptable packs aligns that effort with customer quality; paying for all packs could reward speed and rejects. d Pure piece work gives a strong output incentive but less income stability and may encourage rushing. Basic time pay plus a clear acceptable-output bonus protects a base while retaining incentive, although administration is more complex. Choose the combination because staff value stable earnings and quality matters. Keep targets attainable and check quality; neither scheme guarantees motivation.

blocks.heading: Worked practice: Rewards and their motivational effects
blocks.text:
Tano Packs makes identical packs. Individual acceptable output can be counted, workers control their pace and materials are reliably available. Management compares pure piece work with basic time pay plus an acceptable-output bonus. Staff value reliable income and the customer requires consistent quality.

a Explain how Tano’s reward design could influence effort, cooperation and quality. [8]
b Evaluate whether financial incentives alone are sufficient to motivate this workforce. [12]

a Individual output rewards can encourage pace because workers influence countable acceptable packs. An incentive based only on quantity can divert effort from sealing quality or helping colleagues. A basic payment protects income while a clearly defined quality-and-output bonus aligns the reward with acceptable delivery. Team elements could support cooperation but need fair rules for differing contributions. b Pay reliability and financial reward matter to the stated workforce, and an incentive can make effort worthwhile. However, unfair targets, poor supervision or monotonous work can still reduce motivation. Recognition and suitable responsibility may support satisfaction, while safe conditions and adequate resources remain necessary. Use a fair combination payment scheme with communication, quality safeguards and attention to staff needs, then review results. Do not substitute praise for wages or assume a bonus resolves every source of dissatisfaction.

blocks.heading: Worked practice: Rewards and their motivational effects
blocks.text:
Hema Stitch makes identical items with reliably available materials. Acceptable individual output can be counted and workers can influence it. It compares pure piece work with basic time pay plus a quality-and-output bonus. Staff value stable earnings.

Evaluate pure piece work against basic time pay plus a bonus at Hema. Give a concise plan. [12]

Fit: identical units, reliable materials and controllable output support piece measurement. Benefit: pure piece work makes extra acceptable units directly rewarding. Risk: variable income conflicts with staff’s stated preference and rushing can harm quality. Combination: basic pay offers stability; a bonus can reward acceptable output, with clear rules and more administration. Judgement: prefer the combination because it balances the relevant needs while preserving incentive. Review fairness, quality and whether targets remain under workers’ control.
